newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-BECKER BLAMES "MADHOUSE" ATMOSPHERE FOR DEFEAT.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BECKER BLAMES "MADHOUSE" ATMOSPHERE FOR DEFEAT.

text.p: Boris Becker blamed an atmosphere like a "madhouse" for his shock 6-3 5-7 6-4 second round defeat to Spain's Carlos Moya on Wednesday as he became the sixth seed to bow out of the Paris Open.

The sixth-seeded German, who has won the tournament three times, followed Goran Ivanisevic and Thomas Muster to exit the Bercy contest on Wednesday. Andre Agassi, Wimbledon champion Richard Krajicek and Jim Courier were beaten on Tuesday.
"Coming from a very relaxed atmosphere to a madhouse...that caught me completely off guard," said Becker, who on Sunday won the Stuttgart Open in his home country.
Becker had harsh words for the Paris Open, a tournament he has said in the past he likes and in which he has reached the final five times including last year when he lost to Pete Sampras.
"I felt like I was in a big zoo. Moya and me, we were big gorillas and all around us were some other animals trying to bother us all the time," Becker said.
"I'm extremely disappointed. I mean, I'm still in a state of shock because even though I've played here a couple of times I didn't think it was like that."

Becker, asked what he thought of efforts to encourage young people to go and watch tennis, complained that people were constantly moving and making a noise and there was a huge television camera that also bothered him.
"If this is the way it's going, hopefuly other players will speak up. We're playing with a very small ball and the lines are also very small," the world number three said.
"If people are constantly moving, screaming, laughing, getting up, it's impossible to play great tennis.
"Tennis is not basketball," he said, adding that if perhaps he had been here since Saturday he might have been able to adjust better.

Becker said of his 20-year-old opponent: "He has top 10 potential, but if he wants to progress he should not just play on clay for 10 months. He has to go to a hardcourt season and play indoors more often.
"He played great indoor, serve and volley tennis out there."
Becker said Moya, who he had never played before, said the only reason the Spaniard did not win in two sets was because he was nervous.
Becker could now fail to qualify to defend his ATP Tour World Championship title in Hanover next month. He needed to reach the semifinals to secure his berth in the eight-man event.

Third seed Muster, one of five players who have secured their Hanover places, lost the first set 6-2 to 1990 winner Stefan Edberg before abandoning the match with a hip complaint he said has troubled him since April.
"It's inflamation in the capsule of the hip," Muster said. "And it doesn't look like it's getting better. Resting a little more would help it."
Fifth seed Ivanisevic, who won at Bercy in 1993, lasted only 54 minutes on court in his fifth consecutive defeat to Dutchman Paul Haarhuis, who won 6-3 6-2.
